text: An image tag looks like a version number, but it's really just a mutable label sitting in the registry. Pushing again with the same tag silently repoints it to different bytes, with no warning to anyone pulling it, and latest is the extreme case — whichever push happened most recently — which is exactly why it has no place in a production deployment.

A workable scheme tags one build several ways at once: a full semantic version like one four two for the exact release, floating tags like one four and one that move forward for consumers who want automatic updates, and the short git commit sha so you can always trace an image back to the exact source it came from.

That looks like docker build, then three or four docker tag commands against the same image ID, then a single docker push of the fully-pinned version tag. One build, multiple labels, each serving a different consumer, with no need to rebuild the image just to relabel it.

Pushing to a cloud registry follows the same tag-then-push pattern, but authentication goes through the cloud CLI instead of a Docker Hub login. az acr login against Azure Container Registry, or the AWS CLI's get-login-password piped into docker login for Amazon ECR, each hands Docker a short-lived token instead of a long-lived password.

The one reference that truly can't move is the digest — a sha-two-fifty-six hash of the image manifest, returned on every push. A tag tells a person which release this is; a digest tells the cluster exactly which bytes to run, with zero ambiguity, which is why production manifests increasingly pin to one.

With a real base image, a clean scan, a non-root user, and a traceable tag pushed to a real registry, this image is genuinely production-grade, not just something that happens to run on your own machine. From here, the next chapter moves on to actually running and orchestrating images like this one with Kubernetes.
